config.title: useToggle

intro.title: useToggle
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a custom React hook called `useToggle` that manages a boolean state value and provides a function to switch it between true and false. You will learn the core concept of creating reusable custom hooks to encapsulate and share stateful logic across components. The main technologies involved are React's built-in `useState` hook and TypeScript for adding type safety. By the end, you'll have a practical hook you can use in any React component to easily toggle features like modals, themes, or switches.
intro.usecase: The useToggle hook is a fundamental pattern for managing binary state in interactive UIs across countless real-world applications. You'll see it controlling visibility states for dropdown menus, modals, and side panels in navigation systems. It's essential for toggling between light/dark themes in settings panels, expanding/collapsing FAQ sections on help pages, and switching between edit/view modes in form interfaces. This pattern appears in dashboard filters where users show/hide data layers, in e-commerce sites for comparing products, and in media players for play/pause functionality—anywhere you need clean, reusable boolean state management.

objectives: Construct a custom React hook named useToggle to encapsulate toggle logic
Define TypeScript types for the useToggle hook's return value and parameters
Implement useState to store and manage the boolean toggle state
Apply conditional logic to handle the toggle function's optional parameter
Utilize useCallback to memoize the toggle function for performance optimization
Return an array containing the current state value and the toggle function
Invoke the useToggle hook within functional components to access its functionality
Control component behavior by calling the toggle function in event handlers
Modify the initial state by passing different boolean values to useToggle
Assign the returned state and function to appropriately named variables using array destructuring
Access the current toggle state value to conditionally render UI elements
Handle user interactions by connecting the toggle function to event listeners like onClick

steps.title: Import React and useState from 'react'
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement with curly braces to import both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing React and useState
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The import statement for React and useState is added at the top of the file.
successCriteria: The code includes an import statement that imports React and useState from the 'react' package.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState. This gives you access to React's core functionality and the useState hook for managing state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the import statement needs to include both React and useState from 'react'. Make sure you're using the correct syntax with curly braces.
steps.feedbackWrong: The import statement is missing or incorrect. You need to import both React and useState from the 'react' package using the import statement.

steps.title: Define the useToggle custom hook function
steps.instruction: Define a function called 'useToggle' that takes an initial boolean value as a parameter. The function should be a custom hook (starting with 'use') and use TypeScript syntax.
steps.hint: Create a function declaration or arrow function named 'useToggle' with a parameter for the initial boolean value.
steps.expectedOutcome: A function named 'useToggle' is defined with a parameter for the initial boolean value.
successCriteria: Function has one parameter for initial boolean value
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the useToggle custom hook function with the correct parameter.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've defined a function named 'useToggle' that takes an initial boolean parameter.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Define a function called 'useToggle' that accepts an initial boolean value as a parameter.

steps.title: Add TypeScript type annotation for the initial parameter
steps.instruction: In the useToggle function signature, add a boolean type annotation to the 'initial' parameter.
steps.hint: TypeScript function parameters can be typed with a colon followed by the type, like (param: type).
steps.expectedOutcome: The useToggle function signature should have a typed parameter: useToggle(initial: boolean).
successCriteria: Add boolean type annotation to initial parameter
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added the correct TypeScript type annotation to the initial parameter. This ensures the hook only accepts boolean values.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the type annotation needs to be exactly 'boolean' for the initial parameter.
steps.feedbackWrong: The initial parameter should have a boolean type annotation. Try adding ': boolean' after the parameter name.

steps.title: Initialize state with useState inside the hook
steps.instruction: Inside the useToggle function body, call the useState hook to create a state variable. Pass the 'initial' parameter as the initial state value to useState.
steps.hint: The useState hook returns an array with two elements: the current state value and a function to update it. You can destructure them immediately.
steps.expectedOutcome: The useToggle hook will have a state variable initialized with the value of the 'initial' parameter.
successCriteria: The 'initial' parameter is passed as the argument to useState
The result is destructured into a state variable and setter
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized state inside your custom hook using useState. This creates a reactive boolean value that can be toggled.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're calling useState inside the useToggle function and passing the 'initial' parameter as the initial state value.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Inside the useToggle function, you need to call useState with the 'initial' parameter to create the initial state.

steps.title: Define the toggle function handler
steps.instruction: Inside the useToggle hook, define a function named 'toggle' that uses the state setter to invert the current boolean value.
steps.hint: The toggle function should call the state setter function (the second element from useState) with the opposite of the current state value.
steps.expectedOutcome: The useToggle hook now contains a toggle function that can be used to invert the boolean state value.
successCriteria: The code should include a toggle function definition inside the useToggle hook that calls the state setter with the opposite of the current state value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the toggle function that will invert the boolean state value when called.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're defining a function named 'toggle' that calls the state setter with the opposite of the current value.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Inside the useToggle hook, define a function called 'toggle' that uses the state setter to invert the boolean value.

steps.title: Return the state value and toggle function from the hook
steps.instruction: Inside the useToggle hook, return an array containing the state value and the toggle function.
steps.hint: Use the return statement to return an array with the two values: the current state and the toggle function.
steps.expectedOutcome: The useToggle hook should return an array with the current boolean state and a function to toggle it.
successCriteria: The hook returns an array containing the state value and the toggle function.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully returned the state and toggle function from the custom hook. This allows components to destructure and use these values.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the return statement might be incomplete or incorrect. Make sure to return an array with exactly two elements: the state value and the toggle function.
steps.feedbackWrong: The hook doesn't return the required values. Remember to use a return statement with an array containing the state and toggle function.

steps.title: Add TypeScript return type annotation to the hook
steps.instruction: Add a TypeScript return type annotation of `[boolean, () => void]` to the `useToggle` function declaration.
steps.hint: After the function parameters, add a colon followed by the tuple type `[boolean, () => void]`.
steps.expectedOutcome: The `useToggle` function should have an explicit return type annotation indicating it returns a tuple containing a boolean and a function that returns void.
successCriteria: The function declaration includes `: [boolean, () => void]` after the parameter list
The return type annotation is correctly placed before the opening curly brace
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added the TypeScript return type annotation correctly. This makes the hook's return value explicit and improves developer experience.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the return type annotation needs adjustment. Make sure it's `[boolean, () => void]` and placed after the parameter list.
steps.feedbackWrong: The return type annotation is missing or incorrect. Add `: [boolean, () => void]` after the function parameters to explicitly type the hook's return value.

steps.title: Use the useToggle hook in the App component
steps.instruction: Inside the App component, call the useToggle hook with an initial value of false. Destructure the returned array into two variables: one for the current state value and one for the toggle function.
steps.hint: Call useToggle(false) inside your component and destructure the result like: const [value, toggle] = useToggle(false);
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component now has access to the toggle state and function returned by the useToggle hook.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully called the useToggle hook inside your App component. The hook returns the current state value and a toggle function that you can now use in your UI.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're calling useToggle with false as the argument and destructuring the result into two variables.
steps.feedbackWrong: The useToggle hook needs to be called inside the App component with an initial value of false, and the result should be destructured into two variables.

steps.title: Add a button and wire its onClick to the toggle function
steps.instruction: Inside the App component's return statement, add a button element that displays the current state value and calls the toggle function when clicked.
steps.hint: The button should show the current boolean value from useToggle and have an onClick handler that calls the toggle function.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component will render a button that displays the current boolean state and toggles it when clicked.
successCriteria: Button element exists inside the div
Button's onClick handler calls the toggle function
Button's content displays the isToggled value
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a button that displays the current toggle state and calls the toggle function when clicked.

steps.feedbackWrong: The button is missing or not properly wired. Check that you added a button element with onClick={toggle} and content showing {isToggled}.
